findings.claim: All 42 practice mark schemes run a 20-mark ladder ("Top band (17-20)" ... "Lower band (1-4)") or a 10-mark ladder ("Top band (9-10)" ... "Lower band (1-2)"), while the question label says 40 marks.
findings.truth: The post-1914 play question is worth 40 marks: 16 AO1 + 16 AO3 on a 32-mark grid, plus 8 separate marks for accurate written expression. Rewritten onto the house ladder used for the sister Edexcel post-1914 units: Top band (27-32) / Upper-mid band (20-26) / Mid band (13-19) / Lower-mid band (7-12) / Low band (1-6), then a closing line for the 8 further marks.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md raw-mark table (Questions 7 to 30: AO1 16, AO3 16, AO4 8, total 40); house precedent scripts/_retrofc/units/english-literature-edexcel__the-empress/_edits.json

findings.claim: Three places write an AO code immediately before a full stop: "useful for AO3." (L1), the flashcard answer "AO3." (L3), "across AO1 and AO3." (L6).
findings.truth: The house validator rejects that pattern. Each now reads "AO3 (context)".

findings.claim: Six places name the paper as "Component 1, Section B" (L1 content and exam tip, L4 exam tip, L6 content, L7 exam tip and knowledge check 4).
findings.truth: "Component 1" is a banned spec-code string; the whole unit would fail the house validator. Each now says "the post-1914 play essay" or "the Edexcel post-1914 play question".

findings.claim: "you will be given a quotation from the play and asked to write an essay" - no mention that the paper offers a choice.
findings.truth: Students answer ONE essay question from a choice of two, and each question is preceded by a short quotation from the text as a stimulus.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md Component 1 assessment overview: "students answer ONE essay question from a choice of two on their studied text"; "Each question will be preceded by a short quotation from the text"

findings.claim: "The play opens with Alem and his father, Mr Kelo, arriving at a small hotel in the north of England."
findings.truth: The hotel is Mr Hardwick's, in LONDON. The play does not open with the arrival either: Scene 1 is a flashback of Alem and his father looking at the north star, and Scene 2 is Alem waking alone in the hotel, where Mr Hardwick calms him and hands him the letter.
findings.evidence: https://blended-learning.resources.wjec.co.uk/en/mfw23-24_2-8/ (WJEC blended-learning study pages for the Zephaniah/Sissay play) plot pages; scene-by-scene summaries indexed as "Scene 2 Alem wakes up in Mr Hardwick's hotel in London"; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugee_Boy ("takes him to London")

findings.claim: The unit asserts a three-act structure 26 times, including "Act 3 brings the play's three acts into a clear structure", a practice question on "the three-act structure", a knowledge check on "The play's three-act structure", a matching item with Act 1/Act 2/Act 3, and a flashcard "How are the three acts of Refugee Boy structured emotionally?"
findings.truth: Sissay's adaptation has no acts. It is an episodic, non-linear chain of numbered short scenes (WJEC's own study notes flag "the episodic structure" and "the non-linear plot", and cite "Scene Six", "Scenes 9-12", "Scenes 17-19"), and the premiere ran straight through with no set changes and no interval. In-body references are now neutral (opening / middle / closing scenes). LESSON TITLES still read Act 1/2/3 and are left for the orchestrator.
findings.evidence: https://blended-learning.resources.wjec.co.uk/en/mfw23-24_2-8/ (WJEC blended-learning study pages for the Zephaniah/Sissay play); https://theculturevulture.co.uk/cultures/theatre/refugee-boy-at-wyp/ (review of the 2013 West Yorkshire Playhouse premiere) ("the whole play flowed freely, with no set changes or intermission")

findings.claim: "Mustapha becomes Alem's first real friend in England" at school; Sweeney is defined as "A racist bully at Alem's school"; "school exposes Alem to racism. Some students are hostile".
findings.truth: Alem meets BOTH Mustapha and Sweeney in the children's care home, not at school. Mustapha had himself been bullied by Sweeney there. Alem runs away from the home and is then fostered by the Fitzgeralds.
findings.evidence: https://blended-learning.resources.wjec.co.uk/en/mfw23-24_2-8/ (WJEC blended-learning study pages for the Zephaniah/Sissay play): "Alem is placed in a children's care home, where he meets Mustapha and Sweeney"; "Mustapha was also once bullied by Sweeney"; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugee_Boy ("Sweeney: A bully at the care home")

findings.claim: Ruth is described throughout L3 and L5 as "Alem's social worker or case worker who advocates for him within the asylum system" and as representing "institutional decency"; a practice question asks how she represents "the human face of the asylum system".
findings.truth: Ruth is the Fitzgeralds' DAUGHTER. She shares her home with Alem. She and her father worry that Mrs Fitzgerald will grow too attached, because the family fostered a boy called Themba before and he died. Ruth has no role in the asylum system.
findings.evidence: https://blended-learning.resources.wjec.co.uk/en/mfw23-24_2-8/ (WJEC blended-learning study pages for the Zephaniah/Sissay play) character list (main characters: Alem, Mustapha, Sweeney, Mr Kelo, Mrs Kelo, Mr and Mrs Fitzgerald, Ruth) and plot notes ("Mr Fitzgerald and Ruth worry about what will happen if Alem becomes part of the family and if Mrs Fitzgerald becomes too attached to him"); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugee_Boy ("Ruth: Their daughter")

findings.claim: Alem's mother is named "Mariam" 19 times across L4, L5, L6 and L7, including a glossary term, a knowledge check and four flashcards.
findings.truth: Alem's mother is Mrs Kelo. She is not named Mariam anywhere in the play. "Mariam" is a Refugee Council worker in Zephaniah's source novel, so the name has been imported from the wrong character.
findings.evidence: https://blended-learning.resources.wjec.co.uk/en/mfw23-24_2-8/ (WJEC blended-learning study pages for the Zephaniah/Sissay play) character list ("Mr Kelo, Mrs Kelo") and violence-theme notes ("Mrs Kelo's violent death"); novel study guide indexed as "Mariam and Pamela from the Refugee Council"

findings.claim: Flashcard 7 asks "Which quotation captures the town-wide response to the trauma in the play?" with the answer "Alem must articulate his story to strangers with no personal connection to his suffering."
findings.truth: The question came from a different text - Refugee Boy has no town, and no quotation is given. The answer is about Alem's hearing, so the question has been rewritten to match it.
findings.evidence: internal mismatch; no town appears in any plot summary of the play

findings.claim: Flashcard 5: "What is the name of Alem's mother, who is dead by the play's start?"
findings.truth: Alem's mother is alive when the story opens. She appears in the flashback scenes with the family, and her violent death happens later, after Alem is already in England.
findings.evidence: https://blended-learning.resources.wjec.co.uk/en/mfw23-24_2-8/ (WJEC blended-learning study pages for the Zephaniah/Sissay play) ("The flashback scenes that demonstrate the violence the family were subjected to", "Mrs Kelo's violent death"); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugee_Boy (the father brings news to England)

findings.claim: Flashcard 12 asks "Who wrote the novel Refugee Boy, adapted by Benjamin Zephaniah's stage version?"
findings.truth: The stage version is Lemn Sissay's, not Zephaniah's. The spec lists the set text as the play by Zephaniah adapted for the stage by Sissay, so mis-crediting the adapter is a real risk in an AO3 answer.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md prescribed text list: "play: Refugee Boy, Benjamin Zephaniah (adapted for the stage by Lemn Sissay)"

findings.claim: L4 builds a whole section on "Alem's testimony" before an asylum tribunal panel: "The most powerful moment in the tribunal is Alem's testimony... He describes the violence in Ethiopia, the persecution his family faced...", and two practice questions rest on it.
findings.truth: I could confirm that the play stages a courtroom (the premiere used projection to shift between Ethiopia, London locations and a courtroom) and that Alem is made a ward of court, but I found no source confirming that Alem himself gives a testimony speech to a tribunal panel. Either verify against the playtext and keep, or recast the section around the court scenes that are attested (the ward-of-court ruling and the asylum claim). Not edited.
findings.evidence: https://theculturevulture.co.uk/cultures/theatre/refugee-boy-at-wyp/ (review of the 2013 West Yorkshire Playhouse premiere) ("whether the scene took place in Ethiopia, different parts of London or even a courtroom"); https://blended-learning.resources.wjec.co.uk/en/mfw23-24_2-8/ (WJEC blended-learning study pages for the Zephaniah/Sissay play) Scenes 17-19 ("a ward of court", "he has claimed asylum")

findings.claim: The unit stops at the hearing. It never covers Mr Kelo's return to England, and it never mentions that he is killed. L4 says only "His father is gone", and L2 leaves him "returned to Africa".
findings.truth: In the play Mr Kelo comes to the Fitzgerald household to take Alem back, is told Alem is a ward of court, and claims asylum himself; in Zephaniah's novel he is then shot dead outside the London office of EAST and Alem is granted asylum without him. A 40-mark whole-text essay needs the ending. This is missing content, not a wrong sentence, so it needs authoring rather than a surgical edit. Not edited.
findings.evidence: https://blended-learning.resources.wjec.co.uk/en/mfw23-24_2-8/ (WJEC blended-learning study pages for the Zephaniah/Sissay play) Scenes 17-19; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugee_Boy (ending)

findings.claim: Lesson titles 2, 3 and 4 read "Act 1: Alem's Abandonment", "Act 2: The Foster Family & School", "Act 3: The Asylum Hearing & Resolution".
findings.truth: There are no acts (see F6), and L3's title also names school as the setting for material that belongs to the children's home (see F7). Titles left for the orchestrator as instructed. Suggested: "Leaving: Alem's Abandonment", "Care Home and Foster Family", "The Hearing and Resolution".
findings.evidence: https://blended-learning.resources.wjec.co.uk/en/mfw23-24_2-8/ (WJEC blended-learning study pages for the Zephaniah/Sissay play); https://theculturevulture.co.uk/cultures/theatre/refugee-boy-at-wyp/ (review of the 2013 West Yorkshire Playhouse premiere)

findings.claim: "Sissay shows it as a ugly, casual part of some people's behaviour."
findings.truth: "an ugly". Fixed inside the F7 edit; the lesson teaches AO4 accuracy, so the slip is worth removing.

summary: Set text confirmed as the STAGE PLAY (spec: play, Zephaniah, adapted for the stage by Lemn Sissay). Exam facts verified: one essay from a choice of two, each preceded by a short quotation; 40 marks = AO1 16 + AO3 16 + AO4 8; no AO2, no printed extract, closed book, paper 80 marks in 1h45. The unit treats the play, not the novel, and its exam framing is broadly right (40 marks, closed book, quotation stimulus, AO1/AO3/AO4, no AO2 claim) - but every one of the 42 practice mark schemes ran a 20-mark or 10-mark ladder, and six places carried the banned 'Component 1, Section B' string. The content errors are concentrated in the play's own facts: there is no three-act structure (the play is an episodic, non-linear run of numbered scenes played without an interval), the hotel is Mr Hardwick's in London rather than 'the north of England', Mustapha and Sweeney are met in the children's care home rather than at school, Ruth is the Fitzgeralds' daughter rather than Alem's case worker, and Alem's mother is Mrs Kelo - 'Mariam' is a Refugee Council worker lifted from the source novel. 124 edits across all 7 lessons; two ADJUDICATE items concern the unverified tribunal-testimony section and the missing ending.
